questions.text: Stock records are checked against physical counts on a defined schedule.
Aging stock is reviewed with a named owner and a next action.
Receiving captures quantities, product identity and discrepancies before stock is released.
Unavailable, held and sellable stock can be distinguished in reports.
Inventory adjustments have a reason, supporting evidence and review.
Reorder decisions use a known sales window and current available stock.
Purchasing considers open orders and expected receipt dates.
Category and vendor performance are reviewed before buying.
Stockouts and excess stock inform the next purchasing cycle.
Purchasing responsibilities, spending boundaries and review cadence are clear.
Current SOPs describe the work people actually perform.
Receiving, transfer and reconciliation exceptions have an escalation path.
Operational compliance checks reference the applicable state and license scope.
Records needed for internal review are organized and retrievable.
Corrective actions have an owner, due date and follow-up.
Each shift has clear responsibilities and handoff records.
Staff are trained on current procedures and changes are communicated.
Production inputs, outputs and losses can be traced to a run or batch.
Production capacity and material availability inform scheduling.
Production or service handoffs identify the next owner and release criteria.
Core systems use consistent identifiers for products, locations and records.
Reconciliation differences between systems are investigated before adjustment.
Access reflects job responsibilities and is reviewed when roles change.
Management reports define their source, refresh time and calculation.
Important operational decisions can be explained from an audit trail.
